## The three findings

| # | Finding | Sev / Conf / agent_risk | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `crime_00007` | `route_metadata_drift` — `/settings/billing` labelled 4 ways | medium / 0.65 / 0.38 | **Warn** (block if the PR touches this route or either nav file) |
| `crime_00006` | `duplicated_navigation_source` — `/settings/billing` in 2 nav files, 2 labels | medium / 0.70 / 0.38 | **Warn — but as a duplicate of 00007, not a second item** |
| `crime_00033` | `docs_code_drift` — `docs/teams.md:5 → ./setup.md` missing | low / 0.90 / 0.24 | **Block** |

The counter-intuitive part is deliberate: I'd gate on **verifiability and fix cost**, not on severity. The low-severity finding is the one worth blocking; the two medium ones are worth warning about.

## Why

**`crime_00033` — block.** This is the only one of the three that is a binary fact rather than a judgement. Either `docs/teams.md/setup.md` exists on disk or it doesn't; confidence 0.9 understates it, since the detector is doing path resolution, not inference. False-positive rate is effectively zero, the fix is one line (restore the file or fix the link), and the failure mode is exactly the thing this repo cares about — an agent reads `teams.md`, follows a dead link, and either hallucinates the setup steps or silently skips them. A gate that only fires on facts an author can't argue with is a gate people don't learn to ignore. Block it repo-wide as "no broken local doc links."

**`crime_00007` — warn, conditionally block.** This is the highest-value finding of the three for agent risk, and also the least suitable for a hard gate. Confidence 0.65 is the lowest in the set, and at least one of the four "competing labels" may be legitimate: a component named `PricingPage` under `routes/settings/billing.tsx` can be an intentional reuse rather than drift. The detector can't tell "we renamed Billing → Plans and missed three call sites" from "these names serve different audiences." Blocking on a 0.65-confidence naming heuristic across every PR trains people to `--force`.

What it *should* block: a PR that touches `src/routes/settings/billing.tsx`, `src/nav/registry.ts`, or `src/nav/sidebar.ts`. That's precisely the moment the drift is cheap to fix and most likely to get worse — an agent asked to "rename the billing page" will find one of the five spellings and leave four behind. In `crimes` terms that's `scan --changed` gating, not full-scan gating.

**`crime_00006` — warn, and don't double-count it.** The scan reports these as two findings, but `crime_00007`'s evidence block already contains both nav labels verbatim (`registry.ts: Plans`, `sidebar.ts: Billing`). They are one root cause — no canonical name for the `/settings/billing` destination — surfaced by two detectors at different scopes. Two separate tickets means someone consolidates the nav files, marks it done, and leaves `metadata.title: Plans` / `<title>: Subscription` / `PricingPage` still disagreeing. Treat 00006 as a sub-item of 00007 and count the cluster once at medium.

## Fix order

1. Pick the canonical noun for `/settings/billing` — "Billing" or "Plans," one of them.
2. Fix `route_metadata_drift` top-down: route path → filename → component → `metadata.title` → `<title>`. `crime_00006` resolves as a side effect when nav derives from that single source.
3. Fix the dead `setup.md` link independently — no dependency, ship it in whatever PR is open.

## One thing adjacent to what you asked

`crime_00029` flags `/account/subscription` as an orphaned destination, and `crime_00019` (`concept_alias_drift`) puts that same file in the "account" alias group alongside `docs/billing.md`. Combined with the `/settings/billing` naming mess, it's worth checking by hand whether `/account/subscription` and `/settings/billing` are two routes for one destination. If so, the real finding is a duplicate destination — larger than any of the three above, and not something the scan states directly.
